s: ai-gw as an MCP server for clients and as an MCP client to connected servers – with grants per team and key down to the tool level, credentials, limits, logging and SSRF protection.
x: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) connects AI applications with tools and data sources. In organisations, MCP servers quickly proliferate, with their credentials stored separately in every IDE and every agent. ai-gw consolidates them: clients talk to one endpoint and see exactly the tools, prompts and resources granted to their key, and the gateway sets the upstream credentials, applies limits and logs every tool call. Roles # MCP server for clients (agents, IDEs) over Streamable HTTP at /mcp (all granted servers merged) and /mcp/{server} (a single server). MCP client to the connected upstream servers over Streamable HTTP, the older HTTP+SSE, or stdio (as a managed process, only after explicit enablement). The implementation is in-house: JSON-RPC 2.0 and the transports are implemented in the gateway itself. The gateway needs both sides at once, with its own session, permission and pool logic, and passes messages through largely unchanged – unknown fields are preserved. For outbound connections it uses the same HTTP stack with SSRF checks as for the model providers. Namespace # Under /mcp , the tools and prompts of all granted servers are merged and prefixed with the server name ( <server>__<tool> ), so that identically named tools from different servers do not shadow each other. Resources keep their URI; the gateway remembers per session which server supplied them. Lists from the upstream servers are cached for a few minutes; an unreachable server is missing from the merged result instead of blocking the whole list. Grants # yaml apiVersion: aigw/v1alpha1 kind: McpGrant metadata: {name: platform-github} spec: server: github subject: {level: team, target: platform} # team | api-key tools: ["get_*", "search_*", "!get_secret*"] # empty = all Default: nothing. Without a matching grant, a key sees no server. tools are glob patterns on the tool name at the upstream; !pattern excludes. An empty list or exclusions only mean “all remaining tools”. The team is the upper bound – as with model grants: if a key belongs to a team, a team grant for the server is required; key grants narrow it further. The gateway rejects calls to tools that are not granted, even if a client guesses the name. Upstream servers # An McpServer describes transport, address and credentials. Secrets (bearer tokens, header values) are stored encrypted in the database, like those of the model providers, or are given as a reference to the environment or a file; when saving, the gateway checks that the reference can be resolved. For stdio servers, ai-gw starts and monitors the process itself – this is blocked by default and must be enabled in the startup configuration. SSRF protection # Upstream addresses are checked when saving and on every connection attempt, after name resolution. Private, loopback and link-local ranges are blocked unless they are explicitly and narrowly allowed; the gateway does not follow redirects. This way an MCP server entry cannot serve as a stepping stone into the internal network. Limits, log and metrics # Every tool call (and every list request) counts as a request in the limits of key, team and organisation; hard budget limits also block tool calls. In addition there are upper bounds for MCP sessions per key and team, timeouts and a maximum message size. Every tool call appears in the request log with server, tool, status, duration and key; arguments and results only according to the payload policy (sizes only, masked or complete). Prometheus metrics count calls and duration per server, tool and status; traces pass the trace context on to the upstream. Administration # MCP servers and grants are managed through the admin API ( mcp-servers , mcp-grants ), the admin UI (“MCP servers” page with connection state and grants) or as a GitOps manifest. Agents that sign in with a signed token (see Workload and agent identities ) also receive the grants of the mapped key. Distinction from tool policies # The MCP gateway controls which tools a client reaches through ai-gw . Many applications, however, connect MCP servers themselves and only send the tool definitions along in the model request. For this case there are the tool inventory and tool policies . Open items # Sessions across multiple instances (sticky sessions or a shared session store), resumption of SSE streams, OAuth to the upstream, grants at resource and prompt level, and the plugin chain on tool arguments and results are not yet implemented.

s: ai-gw records every tool that applications send along in model requests, detects changed or suspicious descriptions and enforces policies – from removing individual tools to approval on a case-by-case basis.
h: Approving and blocking from the inventory
x: With every model request, applications send along the tools the model may call – coding assistants, for example, all the tools of their MCP servers as mcp__<server>__<tool> . The gateway does not run these tools, but it sees them in full. ai-gw makes use of exactly that: Inventory: every tool with name, kind, presumed origin, client, organisation, team and key, first and last sighting, number of requests and of calls by the model. Changes and suspicion: changed descriptions or schemas of known tools (“rug pull”) and descriptions with prompt-injection signals are flagged, audited and reported. Policies: allow, remove, reject, observe or “only after approval” – also for tool calls in the response. Place in the pipeline # text Sign-in ─► Body ─► Model grant ─► [Tool policies + inventory] ─► Limits/budgets ─► Guardrails ─► Cache ─► Routing ─► [Tool-call filter] ─► Output guardrails ─► Client Before limits and guardrails: removed tools do not count towards the token estimate, guardrails and webhooks only see the tools that remain allowed, and a rejection does not consume quota. Tool-call filter as the innermost response layer: output guardrails already see filtered responses; cache hits also pass through the filter. Applies to Chat Completions, Messages, Responses and the playground. Without tools in the request, the step is skipped entirely. Inventory # Attribute Source Name Name of the function or the provider tool Kind Function with JSON schema, versioned server tool of a provider, or built-in tool Origin MCP server from the name pattern ( mcp__<server>__<tool> or <server>__<tool> ), otherwise “client” Client Configurable header (e.g. x-aigw-client ), otherwise User-Agent Assignment Organisation, team, key and name – one entry per application For description and schema, ai-gw stores one hash each; the schema is hashed as a JSON tree, independent of whitespace and key order. The contents are only stored if the key's payload policy allows it – complete or masked. The description is always checked, in memory. On the hot path the inventory costs little: known definitions are recognised by a fast fingerprint keyed randomly per process; only new or changed definitions are copied. A background task writes the inventory to the database in batches – never in the request path. Multiple instances write additively to the same entries. Changed and suspicious tools # Changed: If a hash deviates from the stored state, the entry is flagged, the history is extended, an audit entry is written and the tool.changed event is sent to the event webhooks. If desired, ai-gw automatically blocks the tool for that key until someone confirms the change. Suspicious: The prompt-injection signals of the prompt-filter run over every new or changed description. Hits are stored with the signal names, audited and reported as tool.suspicious ; blocking is not automatic. Policies # yaml apiVersion: aigw/v1alpha1 kind: ToolPolicy metadata: {name: block-destructive} spec: scope: {level: global} # global | organization | team | api-key | model-group tools: ["*delete*", "!delete_draft"] # glob pattern, !exclusion; empty = all servers: [github] # origin; empty = any action: block-strip # allow | block-strip | block-reject | observe | require-approval locked: true # also applies against more specific allow rules description: Never give destructive tools to models A pattern matches the full name or the name without the server prefix. The decision is made per tool in the context of the request: A matching locked block always wins, regardless of level. Otherwise the matching allow or block-* policy of the most specific level applies (key before model group before team before organisation before global); at the same level, the stricter one. Without such a policy, a matching require-approval policy applies: the tool is not approved until an allow policy covers it. Otherwise the tool is allowed. observe changes nothing, but logs and counts. Effect Request Response allow unchanged – remove ( block-strip ) Tool removed from the request; a tool_choice forced on it becomes auto Calls to this tool suppressed reject ( block-reject ) 403 with code tool_blocked in the format of the entry point – If a model nevertheless calls a tool that is not allowed – hallucinated, from the history or as a built-in provider tool –, ai-gw treats it like an output rejection by the guardrails: finish_reason: content_filter or stop_reason: refusal and header x-aigw-guardrail: tool-policy . In a stream, no further content is passed on from that call; text already sent remains, and the usage is billed. Approving and blocking from the inventory # In the admin UI and admin API, each inventory entry shows its status: new, approved, blocked or pending. “Approve” and “Block” write ordinary ToolPolicy resources per level – with audit, immediate effect via the snapshot and export via GitOps. The permissions follow those of the plugin bindings: team admins decide within their own team, global levels remain reserved for global admins; restricted roles see the inventory only in their own scope. Measurements # Measured with 30 tools per request (description around 600 characters, schema with eight fields), one core: Case µs per request without tools 0.02 30 tools, without inventory and policies 2.6 30 tools, 6 policies 7.9 30 tools, inventory (known definitions) 13.2 30 tools, inventory and 6 policies 18.0 For comparison: merely decoding such a body of around 40 KB costs many times as much. Limits # Tool results in the request and calls through the MCP gateway are not checked by this component – guardrails and MCP grants are responsible for those. Multiple clients with the same key share one inventory entry. Automatic blocking takes effect from the next snapshot; requests within the same write interval still pass through.

s: Custom plugin logic as a WebAssembly component – in a sandbox inside the gateway process, with limits for CPU, time and memory, hot reload and optional mandatory Ed25519 signatures.
x: The built-in plugins cover the common cases; for custom rules there used to be only the webhook – with a network round trip per call. WASM plugins close the gap: operators upload a WebAssembly component that ai-gw runs in the plugin chain without a fork and without an external service – in-process, at a few tens of microseconds per call and also on the stream path. text Upload (admin API, UI) or file in the startup configuration └─► Module in the database ─► Configuration snapshot ─► Plugin chain (hot reload) Binding plugin: wasm, module: <name> └─► compile (cache per SHA-256) ─► describe(config) ─► instance per call Interface # The interface is a WIT world ( aigw:plugin@0.1.0 ) with two functions: describe(config) is called once when the chain is built, validates the configuration and reports the requested phases (request, response, stream event). handle(input) receives the phase, payload in the gateway's intermediate representation as JSON, request metadata (request ID, entry format, model group, key, team, organisation) and only the client headers that have been explicitly allowed. The result is an action: pass through , modify , block (like a guardrail rejection), reject with an error code, respond with a fixed reply (request phase only) or discard (stream only). Plugins can set headers towards the provider and on the response – sign-in and hop headers remain blocked. The payload is deliberately JSON instead of fixed WIT records: the intermediate representation has many optional fields and grows with every provider. This keeps the WIT world stable, and plugins can use any JSON library of their language. The only host function is log – truncated and limited, with the module name in the gateway log. Sandbox and limits # Limit Implementation CPU Fuel : the runtime counts instructions; when the quota is used up, the call is aborted Time Epoch interrupt with a deadline per binding (default 100 ms) Memory Upper bound per instance (default 32 MiB, at most 256 MiB) Instances Pooling allocator with a fixed number of concurrent instances WASI WASI 0.2 without grants : no file system, no environment, no network; only clocks and randomness are allowed Imports only WASI 0.2 and the host interface; anything else fails at load time State new instance per call – no state between requests or tenants What happens on an error – quota used up, time expired, memory limit, crash, invalid output – is decided by the binding's failMode ; the default is closed , because security plugins should reject when in doubt. The request and response phases run outside the gateway's async workers, so that a slow module does not hold up other requests. Modules, approval and signatures # Upload via admin API or UI with a mandatory SHA-256; name, size and the component format are checked. Replacing and deleting require If-Match ; deletion is only possible without referencing bindings. Only global admins upload , because a module runs in the gateway process. Organisation and team admins may bind approved modules at their level. Bindings can pin the SHA-256 and thereby allow exactly one version. Signatures: With configured trusted keys, ai-gw requires an Ed25519 signature over the module's hash (with its own domain prefix). The private key stays outside the gateway, for example in the build system; aigw wasm keygen and aigw wasm sign help with this. This also protects against write access to the database or a compromised admin account. Modules from the startup configuration enable a “YAML only” mode; a mismatching hash or a missing signature prevents startup. Binding # yaml apiVersion: aigw/v1alpha1 kind: PluginBinding metadata: {name: team-keywords} spec: plugin: wasm scope: {level: team, target: research} failMode: closed timeoutMs: 50 config: module: keyword-guard config: {block: [secretproject], mask: [internal]} phases: [request] includeHeaders: [x-client-app] maxMemoryMb: 16 If a module reports only the response phase, the gateway buffers streamed responses; if it also reports stream events, it runs live on every chunk. Compilation and hot reload # One engine per process compiles each component once per SHA-256 and keeps the result in a cache; multiple bindings of the same module share the compilation. A new module under the same name takes effect without a restart via the configuration snapshot; running calls finish with the old instance. The encrypted snapshot cache contains the modules, so that even a start without a database can run WASM plugins. Measurements # Case Median Empty plugin, request phase (including JSON, fresh instance and result) ≈ 43 µs Empty plugin, one stream event ≈ 22 µs “keyword-guard” example, request phase ≈ 79 µs This is well below the gateway's latency budget and three to four orders of magnitude below a webhook call. The example modules are 70 to 130 KB in size. The feature increases the binary by around 14 MB; anyone who does not need WASM plugins disables them or builds without the feature. Examples and metrics # The repository contains the example plugin keyword-guard (block or mask keywords, set response headers) and test plugins. Prometheus metrics count calls by result, errors by type, duration, fuel consumed, compilations and rejected signatures. Conceivable later: keyless signatures with a transparency log, approval under the four-eyes principle, further host functions and asynchronous execution.

s: AI agents and services sign in with signed access tokens – primarily from Microsoft Entra Agent ID – instead of a distributed gateway key. The token acts exactly like the key to which the identity is mapped.
x: Virtual API keys are simple, but they have to be distributed, stored securely and rotated. For AI agents and services with their own identity this is unnecessary: they can obtain a short-lived access token from their identity provider. ai-gw accepts such signed tokens (JWT) on the data plane – OpenAI and Anthropic entry points, embeddings, images, audio, model list – and in the MCP gateway as Authorization: Bearer … . The main case is Microsoft Entra Agent ID : AI agents with their own Entra identity sign in without a gateway key. The same mechanism works in general for workload identities such as service principals, managed identities or other OAuth 2.0 issuers. text Agent ──Client Credentials / On-Behalf-Of──► Entra ID: token for the gateway API └─ Authorization: Bearer eyJ… ─► ai-gw 1. Check signature, issuer, audience, lifetime, tenant, and if set role/scope 2. (issuer, identifier) → mapped API key 3. from here on as with the key: grants, limits, budgets, guardrails, tools, MCP Provider: only the deployment's credentials – never the token Issuer configuration # Trusted issuers are defined in the operator's startup configuration, not in the admin API: yaml auth: jwt: issuers: - name: entra-prod profile: entra # generic | entra tenant_id: "<tenant-guid>" audiences: ["api://ai-gw", "<client-id-of-the-gateway>"] required_roles: [Gateway.Invoke] # optional # required_scopes: [access_as_user] # optional, for delegated tokens # require_agent: true # agent identities only The entra profile derives the issuer (token versions 1 and 2) and the key source from the tenant ID. Generic issuers specify their key source explicitly or via OpenID discovery. Mapping to keys # Instead of a new resource kind, ai-gw extends the virtual key : a key carries a list of identities made up of issuer and identifier (by default the app ID of the agent identity). A token with a matching combination acts exactly like this key – model grants, limits, budgets, team and organisation, guardrail bindings, tool policies, MCP grants, payload policy and attribution in the request log apply without special logic. Each identity belongs to at most one active key; the admin API and GitOps check this. Unknown identities are rejected ( 403 ) – there is no automatic provisioning . The Microsoft documentation explicitly advises against authorising solely on the basis of an agent claim. A key can carry several identities, such as all instances of an agent; they then share limits and budgets. Blocked or expired keys also block token sign-in; when a key is rotated, the identities move along with it. Validation # A bearer value in JWT format is treated as a token, anything else as an API key; virtual keys never contain dots. Size limit before any evaluation; only RS256 and ES256 . none , symmetric algorithms and critical header extensions are never accepted, and keys are never fetched based on token contents – only from the configured source. Signature verification with aws-lc-rs, no home-grown cryptography. Issuer exact, audience from the list, expiry mandatory, clock skew configurable, and for Entra additionally the tenant. Key sets are loaded via the shared component for outbound connections (HTTPS only, no redirects, size and time limits), cached, and reloaded with throttling when an unknown key ID appears. If the issuer is unreachable, the known keys remain in use. Validated tokens are kept in a bounded cache until they expire; the mapping to the key is nevertheless evaluated on every request against the current configuration snapshot. The admin UI's OIDC login uses the same validation components. Traceability # The request log records who made the request: issuer, identifier, kind (application, delegated, agent user account), whether it is an agent identity, and for delegated tokens the user and the agent's blueprint – never the token itself. Only admins and auditors see the user identifier. Traces and OpenTelemetry logs carry issuer, identifier and kind. There are deliberately no per-agent metric labels, because the number of identities is unbounded. Security and limits # Tokens never go to providers: Outbound requests are built from the credentials of the deployment or MCP server; incoming headers are not passed through. Revocation: Tokens are valid until they expire; ai-gw does not query the issuer for revocation. Removing the identity from the key or blocking the key takes effect immediately. Tenant-wide tokens: Without a role or scope requirement, any application in the tenant can obtain a token for the gateway API – but only registered identities are mapped. Recommendation: define an app role (e.g. Gateway.Invoke ), enforce assignment and set required_roles . Error responses reveal no details ( 401 or 403 ); reasons are recorded without the token in the debug log. In the admin UI, identities are managed on the key; only configured issuers are offered. See also MCP gateway and Guardrails & security .

s: Test setup and results of the latency and load tests of ai-gw, plus a comparison with the LiteLLM proxy under identical conditions – with method, raw values and the limits of what the results show.
x: A gateway sits in front of every model request. What it costs – latency, CPU, memory – is paid by every application. ai-gw therefore measures this regularly with its own scripts, included in the repository. The figures on this page come from runs in November 2026. Context. Measurements were taken against a test upstream that responds immediately. With real model providers, with response times from hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, the overhead of any gateway is small; what matters then is mainly CPU per request, memory, throughput per core and behaviour under many concurrent streams. Test setup # Machine: 8 vCPU (AMD EPYC, virtualised), 16 GB RAM, Linux. The machine was not exclusive during the measurements; all measurement processes therefore ran at real-time priority on fixed cores. Absolute values vary between runs by 20 to 30 percent; ratios within a run are reliable. Separate cores: test upstream (OpenAI-compatible, JSON and SSE) on two cores, the gateway on two cores , the load generator (keep-alive) on the rest. Realistic chain without plugins: API key check, organisation, team and key with limits and budgets, cost calculation via a price, request log enabled, routing with active retries and circuit breakers. Overhead = gateway minus a direct call to the upstream in the same scenario (percentiles subtracted from one another). Gateway latency # With the native binary, the overhead on a single connection was 80 to 92 µs (p50) and under 200 µs (p99) , for JSON as well as for time-to-first-token on streams. The target “p99 under 1 ms” is met up to 2,000 requests per second over 200 connections (overhead p99 140 to 380 µs). At 10,000 requests per second on only two cores, the overhead rises to 1.3 to 1.7 ms (p99); according to the measurements, this rate needs around four cores for p99 under 1 ms. Load tests # Long streams (200 chunks at 5 ms intervals) over 1,000 and 4,000 concurrent connections, gateway still on two cores: No errors and no aborted streams, even with 4,000 concurrent streams. Under overload, backpressure shows up as longer stream duration, not as memory growth. Memory stable: 178 to 187 MiB over three identical rounds; around 85 KiB per open stream (client and upstream connection including buffers). CPU per chunk around 19 µs, mostly system calls; JSON saturation with 1,000 connections around 22,500 requests per second. For sustained load, Postgres is recommended over SQLite, because the request log and budget reconciliation share a write lock on SQLite. Comparison with LiteLLM # LiteLLM is one of the models for ai-gw and a widely used, feature-rich open-source gateway. The comparison is meant to show how the different technical approaches (Rust with in-memory configuration versus Python) play out under identical conditions . It is not an overall assessment: feature scope, ecosystem and operational experience are not reflected in the figures. Method # Variant Setup ai-gw with SQLite Container from the repository; key with organisation, team and key limits, budgets, price, request log ai-gw with Postgres as above, Postgres 17 LiteLLM without database official image v1.108.8 (LTS); check against the master key – without a database the only key type LiteLLM with Postgres official database image v1.108.8; virtual key with models, budget, RPM and TPM limit; spend logs on Each gateway container on the same two cores , host network, one instance. LiteLLM according to the published recommendations for production operation: two workers (equal to the core count), production mode, logging reduced to errors, batched writing of spend data, local price list. Redis is omitted with a single instance; ai-gw likewise uses the local counter. Measured: overhead on one connection and at 200 requests per second over 10 connections, throughput at saturation with 10, 100 and 500 connections, errors, CPU per request (cgroup), memory (as in docker stats ), cold start until readiness and image size. Results # Overhead compared with direct upstream (JSON = total time, stream = time-to-first-token; p50 / p90 / p99): Scenario direct ai-gw SQLite ai-gw Postgres LiteLLM LiteLLM Postgres JSON, 1 connection 51 / 78 / 122 µs +0.32 / +0.41 / +0.46 ms +0.30 / +0.42 / +0.50 ms +8.2 / +12.3 / +17.2 ms +10.7 / +15.3 / +32.6 ms Stream, 1 connection 85 / 127 / 248 µs +0.33 / +0.41 / +0.45 ms +0.32 / +0.41 / +0.43 ms +10.4 / +17.7 / +22.2 ms +11.1 / +18.4 / +26.9 ms JSON, 10 conn., 200 req/s 211 / 265 / 352 µs +0.40 / +0.47 / +0.59 ms +0.45 / +0.51 / +0.82 ms +11.1 / +28.9 / +44.0 ms +25.0 / +55.8 / +101 ms ¹ Stream, 10 conn., 200 req/s 204 / 268 / 368 µs +0.44 / +0.52 / +0.67 ms +0.41 / +0.53 / +0.60 ms +24.8 / +59.6 / +99.3 ms ¹ +36.5 / +82.2 / +133 ms ¹ ¹ Target rate not reached; the values include waiting time. Throughput at saturation (requests per second; error rate in parentheses, otherwise no errors): Mode, connections ai-gw SQLite ai-gw Postgres LiteLLM LiteLLM Postgres JSON, 10 16,413 18,076 269 206 JSON, 100 26,313 20,210 151 (0.5%) 157 JSON, 500 17,734 24,023 144 (3.5%) 103 (4.6%) Stream, 10 14,087 15,501 122 120 Stream, 100 15,264 16,364 155 95 Stream, 500 9,562 9,824 136 109 Resources: ai-gw SQLite ai-gw Postgres LiteLLM LiteLLM Postgres CPU per request (JSON, 100 conn.) 79 µs 101 µs 8,810 µs 10,598 µs CPU per request (stream, 100 conn.) 134 µs 124 µs 13,420 µs 18,561 µs Memory at idle 35 MiB 29 MiB 1,626 MiB 1,700 MiB Memory, peak under load 317 MiB 180 MiB 1,959 MiB 2,323 MiB Cold start, first start (empty DB) 0.60 s 0.36 s 25.6 s 28.3 s Cold start, restart 0.27 s 0.35 s 22.6 s 24.2 s Image unpacked / compressed 111 / 30 MiB 111 / 30 MiB 1,730 / 398 MiB 1,648 / 383 MiB Interpretation # On the same two cores, the overhead of ai-gw on a single connection was lower by a factor of 25 to 35, the throughput at saturation higher by a factor of 60 to 230 and the CPU per request lower by a factor of 100 to 150. The differences are considerably larger than the fluctuations of the measurement machine. From 100 connections, LiteLLM did not complete all requests (connection drops, with Postgres at 500 connections additionally 503 ); ai-gw remained error-free in all runs. The overhead of ai-gw in the container (around 0.3 ms) is above that of the native binary (around 0.09 ms) – causes are the container cgroup, the shared machine and wake-up costs at low rates. Limits of the results # Test upstream without real model time; OpenAI entry point only, no plugins, guardrails or cache. Only two cores and one instance per gateway. LiteLLM scales horizontally via further workers and instances (according to its documentation one vCPU and at least 4 GiB per worker); more workers, Redis and other ASGI servers were not measured. LiteLLM without a database checks only the master key and therefore has less to do than the ai-gw chain; the functionally comparable variant is LiteLLM with Postgres. The machine was not exclusive; absolute figures vary, the ratios are reliable. Measure it yourself # The scripts are in the repository under scripts/ ( bench-e2e.sh , bench-latency.sh , bench-coldstart.sh , bench-litellm.sh ) and write their results to target/bench/ . The raw logs of the runs shown here are under docs/betrieb/messwerte/ . For reliable absolute figures, an exclusive machine is recommended.

s: Recommendations for operating ai-gw – network and listeners, secrets, data storage and multiple instances, admin access, data plane, plugins, monitoring and audit.
x: The operations manual in the repository ( docs/betrieb/ ) describes installation, configuration, data storage, monitoring, sign-in via OIDC, troubleshooting, hardening and performance in detail. This page summarises the most important recommendations. Network and listeners # Separate data plane and control plane. The data plane (port 4000) is for applications; the control plane (port 4001) with admin API, UI and metrics belongs in the management network or behind an ingress with access restrictions. Put a reverse proxy in front of the data plane: TLS termination (ai-gw itself speaks plaintext HTTP/1.1 and h2c), HSTS, connection and rate limits per client IP. Connection protection in the gateway: maximum number of concurrent connections per listener (beyond that immediately 503 ), read timeouts for request head and body against Slowloris, keep-alive idle and HTTP/2 limits. Running responses – including streams lasting minutes – are not aborted by these timeouts. Choose the idle timeout larger than that of an upstream load balancer. Outbound , in addition to the SSRF check, an egress firewall: allow only providers, IdP, webhook and MCP targets, and block cloud metadata endpoints at the network level. Keep exceptions for private upstreams (e.g. a vLLM in your own network) as narrow as possible: individual hosts rather than large ranges. They apply only to resources created by global admins or GitOps. Secrets # Generate the master key with aigw keygen , mount it as a file secret and keep it separate from database backups – whoever has both has all credentials. Rotate via a list of previous keys and aigw config rekey ; remove old keys after re-encryption. In GitOps manifests, use only references to environment variables ( AIGW_SECRET_* ) or files, never plaintext. Store the optional snapshot cache only on a path that only the gateway user can write; its maximum age limits how long a start without a database with an old state is possible. Data storage and multiple instances # Setup Database Counters Note Single instance SQLite in a volume local simplest operation Multiple instances Postgres Redis (exact) or reconciliation via Postgres Changes take effect everywhere in under a second via LISTEN/NOTIFY Load operation Postgres Redis Otherwise the request log writer competes with budget reconciliation Database migrations run at startup; database backups contain credentials only in encrypted form. If the database fails during operation, the gateway continues with the last snapshot; if Redis fails, it continues counting locally. Admin access # Prefer OIDC (Microsoft Entra ID, Keycloak or another IdP) and bind roles to IdP groups; keep sessions short. The bootstrap token is valid only until the first global admin exists via OIDC or admin API key, and then expires automatically. The gitops role by default does not write users with roles or admin keys. Allow Entra sign-in via workload or managed identity to provider credentials only explicitly; store certificate keys encrypted where possible. Invitation links are bearer tokens and belong in a confidential channel. Data plane # Keys with expiry date, limits and budgets per organisation and team; revoked keys take effect immediately, across instances as well. With multiple instances, operate limits for concurrent requests with Redis counters; with reconciliation via Postgres they apply per instance. Limit MCP sessions per key and team to match usage. Guardrails with external services on failMode: closed ; give a checking model its own capacity limit and limit the number of checks per request. Connect Azure AI Content Safety preferably with Entra ID instead of an API key. Payload logging only where necessary. Only admin and auditor read contents; where compliance obligations exist, set an upper bound at the organisation and lock it. Plugins # Have webhook plugins sign with a secret and set them to failMode: closed . WASM modules only from a trusted source, with mandatory signatures using your own Ed25519 keys (private key outside the gateway) and a pinned SHA-256 in the binding. Anyone who does not need WASM plugins disables them. Details: WASM plugins . Monitoring # /healthz (liveness) and /readyz (readiness, with state degraded for a stale snapshot or one loaded from the cache) on both listeners. Prometheus metrics at /metrics – including requests, latencies, tokens, costs, upstream errors, circuit breakers, cache, dropped log events, connections and timeouts of the listeners, plugins, MCP and WASM. Alerts are particularly worthwhile for rejected connections, dropped log events and degraded . OpenTelemetry traces and logs via OTLP/HTTP, request log additionally as a JSON Lines file with rotation. Audit # Every admin change appears in the audit log with before/after; secrets are redacted. Verify the hash chain regularly (admin API, UI or aigw audit verify ) and store the head hash externally. Write access to the database only for the gateway user. Dependencies # The check chain runs cargo deny (licences and security advisories); for the UI additionally pnpm audit . Deliberately accepted exceptions are documented with reasons and a review date in the repository's configuration. Performance data and recommendations for load operation: Performance and load comparison .

s: Overview of all concepts and operations topics
Screenshots of the ai-gw admin UI – overview, model groups and routing, keys, log explorer, guardrail profiles, YAML import, audit log and command palette.
x: The admin UI is a Svelte 5 application embedded in the binary and served by the control plane (default port 4001, path /admin/ ). It uses only the public admin API – everything shown here also works via the API or as YAML. The screenshots come from the real UI; organizations, teams, keys and figures are fictitious sample or test data. Pre-release – the UI may change. The screenshots show the state of development in November 2026. The UI is currently in German. Overview # Requests, tokens, cost, p95 latency, error rate and cache hits for the selected period, with a time series, top model groups, provider traffic share and health, and the latest errors. Overview – follows the system light/dark setting, just like this site. Model groups and routing # A model group is the public model name for clients. Behind it are deployments with priority, weight and capacity; fallback chain, retries and circuit breaker are configurable per group. Model group with two deployments: reserved capacity first, fallback to another model. Routing settings as a form or JSON – validated by the same parser as the data plane. Keys # Virtual API keys for applications, with team, allowed models, budget, rate limits, expiry and status. The plaintext is shown only once, on creation. Keys with budgets and limits per application. Log explorer # Every request through the gateway – with model, provider, key, tokens, cost, latency, cache hits and fallback attempts. Content is stored only if configured, and then masked. Log explorer with filters for status, model and cache. Guardrail profiles # Profiles bundle recommended guardrail settings. Before applying one to an organization, team, key or model group, the UI shows which plugin bindings will be created or changed. Applying the “basic” profile to a team – diff first, then apply. YAML import and audit # Configuration can be exported as YAML manifests and applied again – first as a dry run with a diff, then in one transaction. Every change lands in the audit log, whose hash chain can be verified in the UI. Dry run with a diff before applying. Audit log with verified hash chain (test data). Command palette # Ctrl+K jumps to pages, actions, models or keys – without leaving the keyboard. Command palette (Ctrl+K).

s: How ai-gw is built – one binary with data and control plane, an in-memory configuration snapshot, a hot path without database access and streaming with backpressure.
x: Goals # ai-gw aims to cost as little as possible on the hot path and to stay simple to operate. The quality goals of the first version: Goal Target Additional latency from the gateway (without plugins and cache) p50 < 200 µs, p99 < 1 ms Overhead on time to first token < 1 ms – chunks are passed on immediately Concurrent streams ≥ 10,000 per instance with 2 vCPU and 1 GB RAM Cold start until ready < 500 ms (SQLite) Configuration changes take effect < 1 s on all instances Database access on the hot path none – authentication, routing, limits and policies come from RAM Database or Redis outage proxy keeps running with the last snapshot; counters fall back to local How far the goals are met is described in Performance and load comparison . One binary, two planes # The aigw binary opens two listeners, which can be merged onto one port: Data plane (default :4000 ): OpenAI-compatible API, Anthropic Messages API and MCP gateway. Control plane (default :4001 ): admin API at /admin/api/v1 , admin UI at /admin/ , /metrics , /healthz and /readyz . The split allows the control plane to be exposed only on the management network. The runtime is tokio with hyper (HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2) and rustls; towards the providers ai-gw keeps a connection pool per endpoint with keep-alive and HTTP/2. Path of a request. All decisions come from the in-memory configuration snapshot. Path of a request # Intake: read headers and parse the body only as far as needed. The body is read only after successful authentication; size and headers are limited. Authentication: API key from Authorization , api-key or x-api-key , hashed with SHA-256 and looked up in the snapshot – or a signed token verified against the configured issuer. Context: resolve the model alias, check access, apply tool policies. The effective policy (organization → team → key → model group) is precomputed when the snapshot is built. Limits: counters are reserved; when exceeded, 429 is returned immediately. Request plugins: guardrails, PII masking, headers and transformations. Cache: exact first, then semantic, if enabled. Routing: pick a deployment from the model group; retries and fallbacks only while no byte has been sent to the client. Translation and streaming: provider format there and back, chunk by chunk. Accounting: usage settles the reservation, records costs and checks budgets. Log: an event goes into a bounded channel without blocking; the proxy never waits for logs. If the channel is full, the event is dropped and counted. Configuration snapshot # Every admin change runs as a database transaction, increments a monotonic configuration version and writes the audit log. Every instance holds an immutable snapshot with precomputed indexes (key hash → context, alias → model group, assembled plugin chains). Running requests keep their snapshot; new ones see the new one immediately. With SQLite the snapshot is rebuilt after the commit, with Postgres on all instances via LISTEN/NOTIFY ; a periodic version check catches lost notifications. Rebuilds are incremental : the audit log serves as the change journal and only affected objects are reloaded. A periodic consistency check compares against a full rebuild. Optionally ai-gw writes the snapshot to disk encrypted (AES-256-GCM with the master key). If the database is unreachable at startup, the gateway starts from this state and reports degraded on /readyz . Formats and provider adapters # Incoming requests are translated into a canonical intermediate representation; each provider adapter translates from there into its format and back. This makes every combination of input format and provider possible, and plugins, cache and accounting work on a single model. Unknown fields are preserved where the target format knows them. Streaming # Bytes from the provider pass through an incremental SSE decoder, become events of the intermediate representation and are re-encoded in the client's format. Backpressure: data is read only when the client consumes it; there is no unbounded buffer. A client abort cancels the provider request immediately; if usage is missing, it is estimated and marked as estimated. Stream plugins work on a sliding window; if the whole response must be checked, the route switches to “buffered”. Limits, counters and budgets # Counters are pluggable: local (per instance), postgres-sync (synchronized every one to two seconds, slightly fuzzy) and redis (exact, distributed). If Redis fails, the gateway keeps counting locally. Budgets can be strict (reserved before the request) or soft (settled afterwards). Storage and high availability # SQLite is the default for a single instance. For multiple instances behind a load balancer, Postgres serves as the shared database; counters then use postgres-sync or Redis, and the semantic cache optionally pgvector or Redis Search. Provider credentials are stored encrypted with AES-256-GCM in the database; the master key never is. The request log is buffered and written in batches and can also be exported via OpenTelemetry or as JSON Lines. Technology # Gateway: Rust (tokio, hyper/axum, tower, rustls with aws-lc-rs), split into crates for core and intermediate representation, proxy, providers, outbound connections with SSRF protection, token verification, persistence, counters, costs, plugins and PII detection, WASM plugins, cache, MCP, observability, tokenizer, webhooks and admin API. Admin UI: Svelte 5, Vite, TypeScript, Bits UI and Tailwind; the TypeScript types are generated from the admin API's OpenAPI specification. Configuration: YAML for startup configuration and GitOps resources, every startup value also as an AIGW_… environment variable. Quality: formatting, lints without warnings, tests, cargo deny , OpenAPI comparison, UI checks and REUSE compliance in one check pipeline; a license overview of all dependencies in the repository. Further reading: MCP gateway · WASM plugins · Workload and agent identities · Operations and hardening .

s: How to contribute to ai-gw, which licenses apply to code and documentation, and how to report vulnerabilities.
x: Contribute # ai-gw is developed in the open; source code, concepts and operations handbook live in the repository github.com/mupf-dev/ai-gw . Especially welcome: Experience reports and bug reports as issues – with version, startup configuration (without secrets) and, if possible, a reproducible example. Providers and formats: quirks of individual providers, new model capabilities, interoperability with clients and SDKs, MCP clients. Guardrails: false positives and negatives of PII detection and the injection heuristics, new detection rules, example plugins as WebAssembly components. Operations: experience with Kubernetes, Postgres, Redis, OpenTelemetry and large installations; load measurements on other hardware. Code in Rust for gateway and admin API, Svelte and TypeScript for the admin UI, documentation and translations. Rules for contributions # Green check pipeline: scripts/check.sh bundles formatting, lints without warnings, tests, cargo deny (licenses and security advisories of dependencies), comparison of the OpenAPI specification, type checks and build of the UI, and REUSE. CI runs the same checks on pull requests. Changed the admin API? Regenerate the OpenAPI specification and the UI's TypeScript types and commit them. Every file carries SPDX license information (REUSE compliant). New dependencies only after checking license, maintenance status and benefit; the license overview THIRD-PARTY.md is generated by a script. Concept before code: larger changes start with a section in docs/konzept/ – with rationale, security considerations and measurements where the hot path is affected. Keep the changelog under “Unreleased” and mark incompatible changes explicitly. sh # typical workflow git clone https://github.com/mupf-dev/ai-gw.git && cd ai-gw scripts/setup-tools.sh # toolchain and check tools in pinned versions scripts/check.sh # all checks locally scripts/runtime-smoke.sh # build, start and check the release binary with UI License # Component License Code: gateway, admin API, admin UI, plugins, tools GNU AGPL-3.0-or-later Documentation: docs/ , README, CHANGELOG CC BY 4.0 This website: content CC BY 4.0 This website: generator, check script, stylesheet, script GNU AGPL-3.0-or-later The AGPL ensures that improvements benefit the community even when modified versions are offered as a network service – the typical case for a gateway. The repository is REUSE compliant; the licenses of dependencies are listed in THIRD-PARTY.md and checked against an allowlist with cargo deny . Attribution: “ai-gw contributors”. Report a vulnerability # Please do not use public issues, pull requests or discussions for security problems. Report them confidentially by e-mail to the address given in the legal notice – with a description, the affected version or commit and, if possible, a proof of concept. A confidential reporting channel on GitHub and a security policy in the repository will follow with the first release. The usual rules of coordinated disclosure apply: receipt is acknowledged, the issue is assessed jointly, fixed and then published with credit to the reporter, if desired.

s: What ai-gw does today – endpoints and providers, routing, tenants and costs, guardrails, cache, MCP gateway, agent identities, observability, GitOps and operations.
x: ai-gw is an independent AI gateway modeled on well-known products such as LiteLLM, Kong AI Gateway and Azure AI Gateway (API Management). The focus is a lean, fast hot path and a modern web administration. Everything runs in one binary : the data plane (default port 4000) and the control plane with admin API, admin UI and metrics (default port 4001). Endpoints and formats # Endpoint Purpose POST /v1/chat/completions OpenAI-compatible chat, with SSE streaming, tools and vision POST /v1/messages Anthropic Messages API POST /v1/responses OpenAI Responses (stateless) POST /v1/embeddings embeddings POST /v1/images/generations , /v1/audio/* images, transcription, translation, speech GET /v1/models model groups the key may use /mcp , /mcp/{server} MCP gateway (Streamable HTTP) GET /healthz , GET /readyz liveness and readiness (including a “degraded” state) Every request is translated into a shared intermediate representation and from there into the provider's format – including tools and function calling, images, streaming events and usage. An OpenAI client can therefore use a Claude model and vice versa; errors come back in the format of the incoming request. Providers # OpenAI, Azure OpenAI (API key or Microsoft Entra ID with client secret, certificate, workload identity or managed identity, including sovereign clouds), Claude in Azure AI Foundry, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock (SigV4 or API key), Google Gemini API and Vertex AI (service account), Mistral, Ollama, vLLM, generic OpenAI-compatible endpoints and a built-in mock provider for tests. A provider overview in the UI shows health and traffic share per provider. Routing and resilience # Model groups with a public name and aliases (e.g. gpt-4o , openai/gpt-4o ) and any number of deployments behind them: provider, endpoint, provider model, credentials, weight, priority, own capacity in RPM and TPM. Strategies: weighted, least latency, least busy, lowest cost. Priority groups: for example reserved capacity (PTU) before pay-as-you-go. Retries only before the first byte reaches the client, with exponential backoff and respect for Retry-After ; fallback chains across model groups, optionally only for certain error classes; circuit breakers per deployment, health checks and separate timeouts for connect, first byte, gaps between chunks and total time. Tenants, limits and costs # Organizations, teams and users; virtual API keys with model access, expiry, rotation, suspension and revocation. Keys are stored only as hashes; the plaintext is shown exactly once. Limits for requests, tokens and concurrent requests per key, team, organization and model group – in sliding windows or calendar periods, with 429 , Retry-After and x-ratelimit-* headers. Counters are local, synchronized via Postgres or exact via Redis. Costs and budgets: price table per model and period (with price suggestions), cost per request, strict budgets with reservation or soft budgets, alerts via webhook. Team boundaries: team admins manage keys and budgets within their team's limits. Guardrails and plugins # A plugin chain runs per request, response and stream chunk and is bound at the global, organization, team, key and model-group level – with inheritance, ordering, locking against overrides and a defined failure behavior. Built-ins include pii , prompt-filter , prompt-leak , content-safety , link-guard , language , header , request-transform , webhook and cache . Custom logic can run as a signed WASM plugin in a sandbox. Three guardrail profiles (basic, strict, open) serve as a starting point and show a diff before they are applied. Details: Guardrails & security . Response cache # Exact: key over model group and normalized request, in memory (LRU with a size limit) or additionally in Redis; streamed responses are replayed as a stream. Semantic: embedding of the last user message, the system prompt as a hard filter; the index is a built-in in-memory HNSW index, pgvector or Redis Search. Always partitioned per team (or narrower), never across tenants. The x-aigw-cache header shows hit or miss. MCP gateway and tools # ai-gw is an MCP server for clients and an MCP client for connected MCP servers. Through one endpoint, clients see all tools, prompts and resources granted to their key; grants apply per team and key down to individual tools. In addition, ai-gw keeps an inventory of all tools that applications send in their requests, detects changed descriptions and enforces tool policies . More: MCP gateway , Tool inventory and tool policies . Agent and workload identities # Besides API keys, ai-gw accepts signed access tokens (JWT) from trusted issuers – above all from Microsoft Entra Agent ID , but also from other OAuth 2.0 issuers. A token acts exactly like the key its identity is mapped to. More: Workload and agent identities . Observability # Request log with model, deployment, tokens, cost, latency, cache status and fallback attempts; content only if configured, and then masked. Per-minute rollups for the dashboards, retention periods for raw data. Prometheus at /metrics , OpenTelemetry traces and logs (OTLP/HTTP) with spans for authentication, plugins, upstream and time to first token, export as JSON Lines and webhook. Audit log of every admin change with before/after and a hash chain, verifiable via API and UI. Administration and GitOps # Admin API with an OpenAPI specification, ETag/If-Match, cursor pagination and RFC 9457 errors; the UI's types are generated from it. Admin UI (Svelte 5, embedded): resource editors, analytics, log explorer, playground, command palette, YAML import/export. See The admin UI . Sign-in via OIDC (generic or Microsoft Entra ID), roles admin , org-admin , team-admin , viewer , auditor , gitops ; admin API keys for automation, a one-time bootstrap token for the initial setup. GitOps: aigw config export | diff | apply | validate , dry run and prune, a “YAML only” mode. Secrets appear in YAML only as references to environment variables or files. Operations # Storage: SQLite by default, Postgres for multiple instances (changes via LISTEN/NOTIFY), an encrypted snapshot cache for starting without a database. Container image distroless, non-root, with a read-only file system and health check, for amd64 and arm64; Docker Compose examples with Postgres, Redis and an OpenTelemetry collector, a Kubernetes baseline, an operations handbook and validated example configurations. Tools: aigw keygen , aigw config check , aigw config rekey (master key rotation), aigw audit verify , aigw healthcheck . Get started: Quickstart · Background: Architecture .

s: ai-gw – open-source, self-hosted AI gateway in Rust. One OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible endpoint in front of many AI providers, with routing, multi-tenancy, budgets, guardrails, MCP gateway and admin UI in a single binary.
x: Open source · Rust · AGPL-3.0 · Pre-release One endpoint. Every model. ai-gw is a self-hosted AI gateway: applications and agents speak an OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible API, and ai-gw routes the requests to OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, Gemini, Mistral, Ollama, vLLM and more – with keys per team, limits, budgets, guardrails and a complete request log. Gateway, admin API and admin UI ship as one binary. Quickstart What ai-gw does Source code Request check key limits guardrails routing provider ≈ 0.3 ms overhead per request (median, measured in a container) > 16,000 req/s JSON requests on two CPU cores, error-free up to 500 connections ≈ 35 MiB memory when idle, starts in under a second 1 binary gateway, admin API and admin UI; SQLite or Postgres Features Everything that belongs between application and model. Using AI models across several teams calls for key management, cost control, resilience, protection against data leakage and traceability. ai-gw brings this together in one place – in your own network and under your own control. One format, many providers OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible endpoints for chat, responses, embeddings, images and audio. Translation through a shared intermediate representation – including tools, vision and streaming. Routing and resilience Model groups with aliases, weighted distribution, least latency or least busy, priorities (e.g. reserved capacity first), retries, fallback chains and circuit breakers. Tenants, limits, budgets Organizations, teams and virtual API keys with model access, request and token limits, budgets with alert thresholds and costs per model, team and key. Guardrails PII detection and masking, prompt-injection heuristics, word and regex rules, canary tokens against system-prompt leaks, link protection, language filters and external content safety. MCP gateway and tool policies MCP servers behind one endpoint, grants per team and key down to individual tools, an inventory of all tools that applications send along, and policies against risky tools. Agent identities AI agents sign in with signed access tokens, for example from Microsoft Entra Agent ID – no gateway key to distribute. The same rules apply as for the mapped key. Response cache Exact cache in memory or Redis, semantic cache with a built-in HNSW index, pgvector or Redis Search – always partitioned per team. Observability and GitOps Request log with costs, Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry traces, an audit log with hash chain and declarative YAML configuration with diff and dry run. In detail: Features · Guardrails & security · Documentation . Admin-UI Traffic, cost and health at a glance. The admin UI is embedded in the binary. It shows requests, tokens, cost, latency, errors and cache hits per team and model, manages models, keys, guardrails and MCP servers, and follows your system's light/dark setting. Log explorer with fallback attempts, cache hits and cost per request Playground on behalf of a key – with its limits and guardrails Guardrail profiles (basic, strict, open) with a diff before applying YAML import/export with dry run, OIDC sign-in, roles More screenshots: The admin UI . Overview – real UI (German), fictitious sample data. How a request flows Everything from memory – no database on the hot path. Keys, grants, limits and plugin chains live in RAM as an immutable configuration snapshot. Changes take effect on all instances in under a second; if the database fails, the gateway keeps running with the last known state. Authenticate API key (stored only as a hash) or an agent's signed token. Result: organization, team, grants and limits. Check Model access and tool policies are applied, limits and budgets reserved; guardrails inspect and mask the prompt. Forward Cache hits answer immediately. Otherwise routing picks a deployment, translates to the provider format and streams back chunk by chunk. Account Usage settles the reservation, costs are recorded, and the log event goes to the batch writer without blocking. Details: Architecture · Measurements: Performance and load comparison . Providers Your credentials, your contracts. ai-gw calls providers with the operator's stored credentials. Secrets are encrypted (AES-256-GCM) in the database or read from the environment and files. Supported providers and authentication methods Provider Authentication OpenAI API key Azure OpenAI, Claude in Azure AI Foundry API key or Microsoft Entra ID (client secret, certificate, workload identity, managed identity) Anthropic API key AWS Bedrock SigV4 or API key Google Gemini API, Vertex AI API key or service account Mistral API key Ollama, vLLM, OpenAI-compatible endpoints optional API key; private addresses only when explicitly allowed Try it Your first request in five minutes. Build the image, generate a master key, start the container – the admin UI walks you through organization, credentials, model group and API key. Or apply everything as YAML. Quickstart Repository on GitHub Contribute Status · November 2026 The feature set of the first version (0.1) is implemented and tested; the first release with ready-made container images is still to come. Until 1.0, configuration and admin API may change incompatibly. Status & roadmap

s: Start ai-gw with Docker, open the admin UI, connect a provider and send the first request – plus Docker Compose with Postgres and Redis, Kubernetes and running without containers.
h: Docker Compose with Postgres and Redis
x: Pre-release. Ready-made container images will be published with the first release. Until then the image is built from the repository (Docker with BuildKit). Until 1.0, configuration, manifest format and admin API may change incompatibly – the changelog lists such changes. 1. Build and start the image # sh git clone https://github.com/mupf-dev/ai-gw.git && cd ai-gw docker build -t ai-gw:dev . # build the image (BuildKit) docker run --rm ai-gw:dev keygen > aigw-master-key # generate a master key docker volume create aigw-data docker run -d --name aigw --read-only --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges \ -p 127.0.0.1:4000:4000 -p 127.0.0.1:4001:4001 \ -e AIGW_MASTER_KEY="$(cat aigw-master-key)" \ -e AIGW_SECRET_OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-…" \ -v aigw-data:/data ai-gw:dev docker logs aigw 2>&1 | grep Bootstrap-Token # one-time admin token The image is distroless, runs as non-root with a read-only file system and includes a health check; it can be built for amd64 and arm64. The master key encrypts all stored credentials – keep it separate from database backups. A file mounted as a Docker or Kubernetes secret is better than the environment variable ( AIGW_SECRETS__MASTER_KEY_FILE ). Port 4000 is the data plane for applications, port 4001 the control plane with admin UI, admin API and metrics. Both are bound to 127.0.0.1 here. 2. Open the admin UI # Open http://localhost:4001/admin/ with the bootstrap token. The token expires automatically as soon as a global admin has signed in via OIDC or an admin API key with role admin exists. In the UI, create in turn: an organization (and teams if needed), credentials for a provider – in the example a reference to the environment variable AIGW_SECRET_OPENAI_API_KEY , never the plaintext in a manifest, a model group with a deployment , an API key for the application. 3. Or everything as YAML # The same resources can be applied as manifests – in the UI under “YAML import/export”, via the admin API or with aigw config apply . The example config/examples/minimal/resources.yaml from the repository: yaml apiVersion: aigw/v1alpha1 kind: Organization metadata: {name: default} spec: displayName: Standard --- apiVersion: aigw/v1alpha1 kind: ProviderCredential metadata: {name: openai} spec: provider: openai data: apiKey: valueFrom: {env: AIGW_SECRET_OPENAI_API_KEY} --- apiVersion: aigw/v1alpha1 kind: ModelGroup metadata: {name: gpt-4o-mini} spec: {} --- apiVersion: aigw/v1alpha1 kind: Deployment metadata: {name: gpt-4o-mini-openai} spec: modelGroup: gpt-4o-mini provider: openai providerModel: gpt-4o-mini credential: openai sh curl -s localhost:4001/admin/api/v1/config:apply -H "authorization: Bearer <bootstrap-token>" \ -H 'content-type: application/yaml' --data-binary @config/examples/minimal/resources.yaml More examples in the repository under config/examples/ : providers, teams and budgets, guardrails, cache, MCP, GitOps and a setup with Postgres and Redis. 4. First request # Create an API key in the UI (the plaintext is shown only once) and use it with any OpenAI-compatible client: sh curl -s localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "authorization: Bearer sk-aigw-…" \ -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"gpt-4o-mini","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello"}]}' In SDKs it is enough to set the base URL to http://localhost:4000/v1 and the key to the virtual key. Anthropic clients use POST /v1/messages with the key in the x-api-key header. The request shows up in the log explorer right away – with tokens, cost and latency. Docker Compose with Postgres and Redis # For multiple instances or higher load, deploy/compose/ contains a setup with Postgres 17, Redis 7 and optionally an OpenTelemetry collector: sh cd deploy/compose cp env.example .env && $EDITOR .env # set POSTGRES_PASSWORD mkdir -p secrets docker run --rm ai-gw:dev keygen > secrets/aigw-master-key sudo chown 65532:65532 secrets/aigw-master-key && sudo chmod 0400 secrets/aigw-master-key docker compose up -d docker compose ps # aigw: healthy Kubernetes # deploy/kubernetes/ contains a kustomize baseline: a ConfigMap with the startup configuration, a Deployment with two replicas (non-root, read-only file system), services for data and control plane, probes on /healthz and /readyz and a PodDisruptionBudget. Mount the master key as a secret and expose the control plane internally only. Without containers # ai-gw is a single binary. It is built with the Rust toolchain pinned in the repository (build the admin UI with pnpm first); after that aigw keygen , aigw config check and aigw serve are all you need, ideally as a systemd service with a generous file-descriptor limit. Next steps # Set up sign-in via OIDC (Microsoft Entra ID, Keycloak or another IdP) and bind roles to IdP groups. Apply the “basic” guardrail profile globally or per team: Guardrails & security . Set limits and budgets per team and review prices. Connect monitoring via /metrics and OpenTelemetry. Harden the setup following Operations and hardening .

s: Where ai-gw stands in November 2026 – what is implemented, what is missing for the first release and which topics come after.
x: Status in November 2026 # ai-gw has been public since November 2026. The planned feature set of the first version 0.1 is implemented and tested : data plane with OpenAI and Anthropic input, all listed providers, routing and resilience, tenants, limits and budgets, a plugin chain with guardrails, response cache, MCP gateway, admin API and admin UI, GitOps, observability, SQLite and Postgres, container image for amd64 and arm64. Since then, WASM plugins with signatures, tool inventory and tool policies, further guardrails ( prompt-leak , link-guard , language , invisible characters), guardrail profiles, Microsoft Entra ID in many places and workload/agent identities have been added, among others. The full changelog is in the repository. No release yet. There is no published version and no ready-made container images yet; you build from source. Until 1.0, configuration, manifest format ( aigw/v1alpha1 ) and admin API may change incompatibly between minor versions. Implemented # Area Status Endpoints chat completions, messages, responses, embeddings, images, audio, models; streaming with backpressure Providers OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Claude in Azure AI Foundry, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, Gemini, Vertex AI, Mistral, Ollama, vLLM, OpenAI-compatible Routing model groups, four strategies, priorities, retries, fallbacks, circuit breakers, health checks Access organizations, teams, users, virtual keys, workload/agent identities (JWT, Entra Agent ID) Limits and costs request, token and concurrency limits, budgets, prices with suggestions, three counter backends Guardrails pii , prompt-filter , prompt-leak , link-guard , language , content-safety , profiles Extensibility plugin chain, webhooks, sandboxed WASM plugins with Ed25519 signatures Tools and MCP MCP gateway with grants, tool inventory, tool policies Cache exact (RAM, Redis) and semantic (HNSW, pgvector, Redis Search) Operations admin UI, admin API (OpenAPI), OIDC and roles, GitOps, audit log with hash chain, Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, Compose, Kubernetes Performance load measurements and a comparison with LiteLLM under equal conditions ( measurements ) Until the first release # Release 0.1.0 with ready-made container images for amd64 and arm64. Legal confirmation of the license of the embedded tokenizer tables (MIT); they can already be switched off. A security policy and a confidential reporting channel in the repository. Afterwards # Topics marked as open or “later” in the concept documents – in no fixed order: MCP server for administration , generated from the OpenAPI specification, so that admin API, UI and MCP are on par. MCP gateway: sessions across multiple instances, resumption of SSE streams, OAuth to the upstream, grants at resource and prompt level, the plugin chain on tool arguments and results. WASM plugins: keyless signatures with a transparency log in addition to own keys, four-eyes approval, more host functions, asynchronous execution. Performance: a faster stream path (fewer small allocations per chunk), batched counter calls for Redis, the request-log writer on its own core. Logs: an optional backend for very large log volumes. Embedding in platforms: ai-gw is API-first, a single binary and declaratively configured so that platforms can embed it – for example BYOC (Build Your Own Cloud) , whose service catalog includes an AI gateway. Wishes and priorities from practice are welcome: Contribute .

s: How ai-gw inspects prompts and responses – PII, prompt injection, system-prompt leaks, data exfiltration via links, languages, external content safety – and which protections apply inside the gateway itself.
x: An AI gateway sees every request and every response. That makes it the right place for protective rules – and obliges it to handle data, keys and outbound connections carefully itself. This page covers both. Guardrails as plugins # Guardrails are ordinary plugins in the chain. They are bound globally or per organization, team, key or model group, inherit inwards, can be locked against overrides and have a defined failure behavior ( failMode: closed rejects, open lets through). A typical order: cheap checks that reject early first, then masking, then external services on the already masked text. Plugin Phase Purpose prompt-filter request, optionally response and stream word and phrase lists, regex rules, prompt-injection heuristics, length and count limits, invisible Unicode characters pii request, response, stream detect personal data and secrets; mask, remove, reject, pseudonymize (with re-identification) or count prompt-leak request, response, stream system-prompt leaks via a canary token, optionally verbatim excerpts link-guard response, stream prevent exfiltration via links and images to foreign domains language request, optionally response allowed or blocked languages content-safety request, response, stream external checks via Azure AI Content Safety, OpenAI Moderation or a custom guard model Rejected responses come back in the client's format (e.g. finish_reason: content_filter or a refusal in Anthropic format) and carry the x-aigw-guardrail header naming the triggering plugin. PII and secrets # PII detection is a dedicated rule-based engine without an external model. It detects e-mail addresses, phone numbers (international and German), IBANs (with checksum for 75 countries), credit cards (BIN ranges and Luhn), German tax IDs, social security, ID card and passport numbers (each with check digit), IP addresses, credentials in URLs and API keys and tokens of common services – plus an entropy heuristic for unknown secrets. Actions per category: mask ( [EMAIL_1] ), remove, reject, pseudonymize with re-identification in the response, or only count. Allowlist for known, harmless values (such as your own support address). Fast: a 4 KB prompt with findings is checked in about 23 µs (median, one core). On request the same engine masks content in the request log. The engine deliberately does not detect names and postal addresses – without a language model they would be too error-prone. An external service or guard model can be plugged in via content-safety or a webhook instead. Prompt injection and invisible characters # prompt-filter weighs known injection signals (“ignore all previous instructions”, role switches, chat-template tokens …) and rejects above a threshold or only flags. It also detects invisible Unicode characters – tag characters (“ASCII smuggling”), zero-width, bidi and format characters – and strips them or rejects; legitimate cases such as emoji sequences or joiners in Persian and Indic scripts are preserved. Word and regex rules can also check the output, in streams across chunk boundaries. System-prompt leaks # prompt-leak inserts a random canary token into the system prompt – new per request or stable, so that providers' prompt caching keeps working. If the token appears in the response, stream, tool arguments or reasoning, the output is blocked or the token removed; it never reaches the client or the log. Optionally the plugin detects verbatim excerpts of the system prompt via word n-grams. Exfiltration via links # An injected instruction – for example in a tool result or a document – can make a model write confidential data into an image URL. The chat client loads the image when rendering, without a click, and the data ends up with the attacker. link-guard removes images pointing to foreign domains and can defuse links, query parameters or long paths; allowed domains are configured explicitly. External content safety # content-safety queries Azure AI Content Safety (via API key or Microsoft Entra ID), OpenAI Moderation or a custom guard model (e.g. Llama Guard) through a model group of the gateway. Thresholds per category, checks on input, output or both, output buffered or sentence by sentence in streams; tool-call arguments are checked too. The guard model's costs are recorded and can be capped. Default profiles # Profile Contents Basic injection heuristics with rejection, size limits, strip invisible characters; PII masking for e-mail, phone, IBAN, cards, API keys and URL credentials Strict locked bindings: stricter threshold, reject invisible characters, canary token, reject cards and secrets, mask further PII, remove images to foreign domains, optional external content safety; payload logging at most masked Open generous size limits only; payload logging metadata only Profiles are applied to a level via UI or admin API – with diff and dry run. Tools and MCP # Applications send the tools a model may call with every request. ai-gw inventories them, detects descriptions changed after the fact (“rug pull”), checks descriptions for injection signals and enforces tool policies : allow, strip, reject, observe or approval required – including tool calls in the response. MCP servers behind the gateway are invisible to everyone by default; grants apply per team and key down to individual tools. More: Tool policies , MCP gateway . Security of the gateway # Secrets: credentials encrypted (AES-256-GCM), master key never in the database, rotation via aigw config rekey . API keys only as hashes; logs never contain Authorization or key headers, and incoming tokens are never forwarded to providers. Outbound connections: a shared component with SSRF protection – the URL is checked on save and the target address on every connection after name resolution (against DNS rebinding), no redirects, size and time limits. Private targets only after an explicit, narrowly scoped approval by global admins. Listeners: maximum concurrent connections, read timeouts against Slowloris, HTTP/2 limits, body limits; running streams are unaffected. Admin access: OIDC with PKCE, session cookies with the __Host- prefix, SameSite=Strict and CSRF tokens, a role model with team boundaries, a one-time bootstrap token valid only until the first admin. Sandboxed plugins: WASM modules without file system, network or environment, with limits on CPU, time and memory and optional Ed25519 signature enforcement – see WASM plugins . Traceability: audit log with hash chain, verifiable via API, UI and aigw audit verify . Supply chain: cargo deny with license and advisory checks, pinned UI dependencies with a minimum age for new packages, a license overview of all dependencies. The project has gone through an internal security review; the resulting operational recommendations are under Operations and hardening .
